game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
It's 5 minutes into the future, in a fictional nation where you have just joined a secret government organization whose job it is to gather information, sometimes publicly available, sometimes deeply private and personal, and use it to prevent and solve crime.

Your job is to rifle through this information and pass snippets of it that you deem important to the case over to your superiors, who will constantly give you feedback and requests for more. It doesn't take long before you realize that this is a horrible system where your personal opinions and feelings can decide what picture is painted of the people you investigate, and that "Nothing to hide, nothing to fear" is as empty and absurd as saying that only troublemakers need freedom of speech or personal lives. And your superiors are constantly suspicious of everyone.

Facebook posts deleted after the medicated user had an outburst...nothing to hide, nothing to fear.
Take statements out of context and ruin peoples lives with them...nothing to hide, nothing to fear.
Cherrypick contradicting statements and go with the interpretation you feel like. Did the attack happen in defense, or out of anger? Nothing to hide, nothing to fear.
Cause tension in a relationship by reporting the theft of a credit card that one had willingly lent to the other. Nothing to hide, nothing to fear.

Thanks for reading my review, NSA.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
[b]My playtime:[/b] 10h (based on steam, 100% achievement; 2.5x playthrough)
[b]Grindy Achievement(s):[/b] No.
[b]Optional Achievement(s):[/b] Yes (17 achievements).
[b]Difficult Achievement(s):[/b] No.

[h1]Intro[/h1]
[i]Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You[/i] is a massive information gathering system where you, an investigator, is taking a role in sorting the relevant data and fix conflicting data that the system gathered to assist a crime. The game has story branching that persists over 5 chapters.

[b]Pros:[/b]
- 5 chapters
- Multiple endings and story branching that persists over the chapters
- Clean and fresh-looking interface
- You can restart a chapter after you finished the game

[b]Cons:[/b]
- Phone calls and chat animations take a very long time to finish
- Some clues are too hard to deduce unless if you know the full story
- You can't press the button to show conflicting data sometimes

[h1]Should you buy this game?[/h1]
[b]Yes.[/b]
[i]If you like to read or stalk people, you should buy this game. You also can buy it at a discount if you think that the playtime isn't worth the full price.[/i]

------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
[h1]In-Depth Review[/h1]

[h1]Graphics[/h1]
The interface is clean and fresh-looking. I like how the summary that is shown at the end of the chapter is introduced; it looks like the workboard in my office except that it's way cleaner.

As someone who likes to try something by doing it firsthand, I don't find the design to be confusing. The portal section looks like your regular website, the message section looks like your regular chat app, and the device section looks like the simpler version of your device.

I'm also impressed by how the dev showed the photos; it looks like a fragmented version of our faces and it looks so detailed even though it's not. The important facial like eyes and hair is shown although most details are blurred and fragmented.

The cutscene at the prologue skipped a few frames to me though, although I don't have any trouble in understanding the story because of that.

[h1]Story[/h1]
The story is being told by several conversations of your "adviser", someone who deduce things based on your findings, and whatever you read when you try to find clues, which are mostly from chat and phone calls.

Even though most conversations are held this way, I didn't find the main story to be confusing. Even if you couldn't understand the story, the "adviser" will give you some sort of info as to what is happening so you should be fine as long as you don't skip it. There's also a summary at the end of the chapter if you want to keep track of things.

There are several branchings in the game, either minor or major. I find the conversation between the branches to be smooth although some parts confused me since I didn't know the whole story at that moment. You need to play several playthroughs throughout the game to get all the major story branches and understand the whole story.

The thing is, there is no good or bad ending in this game; it's all about your opinion. You think what you think is good and bad. You also can deduce the whole story if you want or you can just understand the main story and be done with it.

[h1]The game[/h1]
[b]Features[/b]
There are 3 sections where you do most of your work: portal, message, and device. The in-game name is different, but I can't seem to recall the actual name since you don't need to know about the name to use it.

The portal consists of several web pages that you can access. The pages that you can access are limited to the system and more will show up as you unlock more clues.

The message, on the other hand, is a bit different. A message, either chat, email, or phone, will show up at certain times and you're allowed to wire-tap their chat and calls in real-time. The thing is, the chat speed is very slow. You can speed up the phone chat speed a bit although I still want it to be faster. It's taking too much time to listen to it especially when you're replaying your playthrough.

The device can be activated after you obtain a serial number of the target's device. You can access all files in the device, whether it's from a desktop or phone.

[b]Investigation[/b]
The suspect will have a profile page that you can fill with data. These data can be obtained by browsing through the 3 sections I mentioned. The data that you can take will be highlighted, either in blue or yellow.

Blue-colored means that there is no conflict with the data and yellow means that the data contradicts with other data. The game also has an option to show the conflicting data although I find that it's not working sometimes.

The thing is, you have freedom in choosing whatever you submit. I thought that I should fill all of the highlighted data in blue for complete profiling, but it's actually the opposite. All the data that you fill will be useful for the advisor's judgment and other people's fate, so you should decide carefully on what you submit.

Some data that you submit will change the story greatly, some are not. However, there are times where you have to make a major guess in determining the conflicting data that you must submit because you didn't know much and the clues are too vague at that point. Luckily, as I said before, there are no good and bad endings, so you can proceed as you please.

[b]Replayability and Length[/b]
As I said before, there are multiple endings. There are 5 chapters in total and each chapter except the last one lasts around 1 hour. I played the game fully twice and played one last playthrough from chapter 3 to unlock all of the major branching and achievement. It took me around 4 hours to finish all chapters at once.

Each chapter has a minimum of 2 endings that will affect the subsequent chapter. You can restart the whole story from the beginning or replay the chapter if you want after you finish the game once. Restarting the game from a specific chapter will delete all of the subsequent chapter data though.

[h1]Conclusion[/h1]
It's a nice game where you have to browse through things and wiretap people's communication to find out whatever is going on. The game has a lot of story branching and replayability.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
[h1]Description[/h1]

Orwell is a visual novel that puts you in the shoes of a Big Brother employee: you are tasked with spying on people and uploading to the system anything suspicious. Unlike most visual novels, you are not presented here with walls of text followed by lists of choices. Rather, your interaction with the game and its unfolding story goes solely through the gimmick of uploading the data chunks you find (or not). By picking among conflicting data chunks or by choosing not to upload some sensitive information, you impact the story in small and big ways.

[h1]Pros[/h1]
[list]
[*] Fresh interaction gimmick that goes very well with the theme
[*] Credible writing with many characters each having their own style of speech
[*] Interesting choices going WAY beyond the good/bad dichotomy
[*] Decent art style
[*] Fair amount of consequences to choices made, though the game remains linear
[/list]

[h1]Cons[/h1]
[list]
[*] Notification system takes some getting used to ([spoiler]the system will sometimes find old information suddenly relevant, requiring you to regularly browse through the lists of documents to make sure no red star has popped[/spoiler])
[*] Because all chats and phone calls are delivered sloooooowly (and I found no way to speed them up), replaying the game to get the achievements or test other choices is a bit of a chore
[*] Political messages are (very) thinly veiled and might annoy (or even anger?) some players
[/list]

[h1]Verdict[/h1]

Do you hate it when someone tries to convey a political message artistically and ends up as subtle as a bull in a china shop? If so, stay away from this game. You're going to hate it.

Still here? OK, here's an idea: put yourself in the shoes of an orwellian enforcer and imagine the consequences of government trampling all over freedom, privacy and presumption of innocence.

Interested? Then try Orwell. Go in expecting a fresh visual novel and a politically charged (to the point of being heavy-handed at times) thought experiment. There is much to like.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
In Orwell you take the role of an investigator working for the government to investigate a series of terror attacks.

Throughout the game you are presented with lots of pieces of information which you have to upload to a person's "file" to establish a character background to see if they're involved in the terror attacks. I found this gameplay mechanic to be thrilling. You tap phones, computers, emails - pretty much everything! At points you are presented with conflicting information between the suspects. This is were the story can change. In a sort of telltale like manner, your choices affect the outcome of the game and your consequences are final. 

I really enjoyed this game and found myself enagaged with each episode. I do wish it was longer, or maybe had some DLC cases added.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Orwell: Keeping An Eye On You (in short, Orwell) is a five-part episodic narrative-driven mystery video game by Osmotic Studios set in a dystopian world in which the player assumes the role of a governmental operative who monitors surveillance sources to discovery national security threats. The game is named after the famed anti-totalitarian writer George Orwell and is inspired by themes established by his magnum opus novel, 1984.

The story in Orwell takes place in a country named The Nation which is governed by a contemporary authoritarian government known as The Party. Due to a series of events in the past, The Party passed the Safety Bill which expanded the government's capability to spy on its citizens in the name of national security. To accomplish this, the Ministry of Security, at the helm of Secretary of Security Catherine Delacroix, built a secret surveillance system codenamed Orwell. After a successful application and being selected from a pool of candidates, the player takes the role of an outsourced Orwell investigator who lives outside The Nation and is tasked, with the help of an assigned advisor going by the alias of Symes, to find evidence on the terrorist (individual or group) who caused a bomb explosion during a presumably peaceful protest in the populated Freedom Plaza in Bonton, the capital city of The Nation, destroying a statue and killing several people. The player soon stumbles upon an activist group called Thought who advocates for freedom of speech with anti-governmental sentiments, yet unaware of Orwell, who is entangled in the bombing incident. From there on, the player uses everything at their disposal to find evidence to expectantly incriminate their first suspect, Cassandra Watergate, an artist who was present at the Plaza shortly before the explosion.

The story occurs across five days (episodes) and what originally seemed like another day at the office, turns into an intricate roller-coaster of a journey full of conspiracy theories, deception and shocking revelations. The narrative in Orwell is exceptionally well-written and what keeps the player on their toes and constantly engaged. Just as things might get slightly monotonous now and again, the story always seems to throw you a new bone through unexpected plot twists and interestingly branched out paths shaped by your various choices and consequences. Even though the story occurs across a country, Orwell actually focuses on a small group of individuals despite the illusion it might give in the beginning, thus I did end up wishing more citizens were actually involved in the end. Whilst this is somewhat disappointing, it makes for a more focused story and does help to get better attached to those said characters, which Orwell succeeds in both aspects. Frankly, the overarching story and its thought-provoking themes, along with the interesting characters you encounter along your journey, albeit a touch stereotypical once in a while, are the selling points of Orwell, and I am delighted to report that it satisfied my itch for a robust adventure mystery game which I have not had for a while recently. Due to the nature of the game, I cannot talk more about the story nor discuss its outcomes at this point, as it is best to unravel and experience it yourself, but there are about four confirmed endings. The game’s length lies somewhere between 4 – 6 hours, which I personally completed in one sitting thanks to its captivating story which made me impatiently want to know what happens next, but I do wish it were longer.

All in all, Orwell's gameplay is akin to a visual novel, so there is not a lot of interactivity involved, but what it does, mechanically speaking, is very solid and straightforward. During investigations, the player has to do various tasks such as (1) browsing and reading through news articles, social media pages and databases, (2) hacking computers or mobile phones to access stored data, and (3) wiretapping conversations over the phone and messaging applications. Each one of these tasks displays various text passages in the form of datachuncks (highlighted by the game for the player’s ease) which could be uploaded on the surveillance system to piece together clues, construct evidence on suspects and, in theory, incriminate them. Each new datachunck uploaded updates a suspect’s profile with more information and occasionally even opens up profiles of new suspects in connection to the respective suspect as the plot thickens. You cannot undo an upload, so think carefully beforehand. Sometimes suspects give contradicting statements over the duration of the story through either dishonesty or unintended misinformation as the result of human nature, which you would then have to use your own judgement and decide which datachunck to upload to support the government’s case, or not. You see, the player can play by the rules to appease the government or ignore vital information to protect the suspects (depending on your moral compass), and either playstyle has several cleverly written consequences. The mechanics do feel too simplistic and repetitive but begin to shine in the second half of the game once there is a lot more information to chew and digest. Moreover, the adviser gives you bite-sized info as to what is happening during almost each one of your moves, so technically you should not feel lost with how the story unfolds. Plus, at the end of each day, a window summary displays all your findings and events that occurred on the day to be up to speed.

One major criticism I do have with its gameplay, however, is that despite the game warning the player that they are not required to upload every datachunk spotted, I always had the compulsion to upload everything I could find regardless since there is no penalty for doing so as far as I recall, aside for a handful of contradictions and, of course, the path of some key plot events. Retrospectively, I feel the game should have better incentivised the player to upload fewer datachuncks or increased contradictions to spice things up. Unfortunately, the game limits your number datachuncks uploads to create a nerve-wracking atmosphere (commendable mechanic) only at the end and I wish that was predominant throughout the entire game instead.

Visually, Orwell is all about the graphical user interface (of a computer monitor) since that is where you will be carrying out all your investigations and decision-making. The art style with its stylized polygonal pictures suits its dystopian themes and the presentation is sufficiently appealing thanks to its good use of appropriate colour pallets and well-designed page layouts. The interface is also intuitive and easy to navigate as a result of its slick design. Whilst the soundtrack is rather short and may seem minimal, it brilliantly captures the eerie atmosphere and even gets momentarily tenser when a plot twist occurs and stakes have risen. Considering there is plenty of reading and no voice acting involved, the tone and vibe of the soundtrack help it to never become distracting.

In conclusion, Orwell: Keeping An Eye On You is a fantastic, but short, mystery game set in a frightfully believable dystopian setting with a strong narrative that challenges your own ethics and presents balanced points of view in the long-lasting battle between the individual’s freedom and privacy versus the government’s security and surveillance. Whilst it is mechanically simplistic and not as diverse, nor challenging, as a game like Papers Please which shares a few familiar social commentaries, it is unique in its own right and worthy of a spiritual successor to 1984. At the end of the day, it is an interactive book more than a conventional adventure game where you might solve puzzles, which feels appropriate considering it is inspired by a novel. Definitely a must-play for George Orwell fans like myself and anyone interested in good mystery/detective games in the format of visual novels.

Stay vigilant.

The art style with its stylized polygonal pictures suits its dystopian themes and the presentation is sufficiently appealing thanks to its good use of appropriate colour pallets and well-designed page layouts. The interface is also intuitive and easy to navigate as a result of its slick design. Whilst the soundtrack is rather short and may seem minimal, it brilliantly captures the eerie atmosphere and even gets momentarily tenser when a plot twist occurs and stakes have risen. Considering there is plenty of reading and no voice acting involved, the tone and vibe of the soundtrack help it to never become distracting. In conclusion, Orwell: Keeping An Eye On You is a fantastic, but short, mystery game set in a frightfully believable dystopian setting with a strong narrative that challenges your own ethics and presents balanced points of view in the long-lasting battle between the individual’s freedom and privacy versus the government’s security and surveillance. Whilst it is mechanically simplistic and not as diverse, nor challenging, as a game like Papers Please which shares a few familiar social commentaries, it is unique in its own right and worthy of a spiritual successor to 1984. At the end of the day, it is an interactive book more than a conventional adventure game where you might solve puzzles, which feels appropriate considering it is inspired by a novel. Definitely a must-play for George Orwell fans like myself and anyone interested in good mystery/detective games in the format of visual novels. Stay vigilant.

[h1]General[/h1]

This is [b]not really a game.[/b] Most of the time you would only be pointing out "data chunks" to relevant character, and the said data chunks has been conveniently pointed out to you by the highlight, so you can't miss it. The only time you get a little pressure is on the final episode, when there are "data upload" limit imposed on you.

[h1]There is minimal gameplay[/h1]
There is minimal gameplay, as it is mostly just drag and drop something. The clues are too easily pointed out to you. Sometimes there are some conflicting data, but it is easy to resolve this kind of things. It is also bad that you don't know how the data chunks you are given is processed. A wrong data chunk could suddenly net a very violent response although previous data chunks you have given it is not the way. 


[h1]Story-Rich Gameplay[/h1]
However, the story in the game is excellent. It is not overly long and complicated, but it is quite complicated enough to keep you guessing on who is who and what is the truth beneath all of these things. All of the characters are alive, and the way they are chatting with each other, with you snooping in, at times make you guilty for snooping on someone's conversation. You will also see another person's life, and at times you will feel guilty that you are the one that send them into prison, sometimes by bending the truth so they can be arrested. And seeing their hobbies and their life, but watching their conversation, their blogs, or their social medias, sometimes makes you really hopeful that this guy/girl is not guilty so you could release them, and make you guilty if you have to arrest them.

[h1]Politics and Mass Surveillance[/h1]
Of course, this game is quite a political game, on the issue of mass surveillance. It subtly asks the player on how far the government could go in the name of security, and how is privacy should be treated if you have connection with a terror group. The game beautifully does not refer to any country or any political party (though a subtle jab at "Freedom" and "Peacekeeping" is done). 

Overall a beautiful game.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
[h1] How far are you willing to go to protect the populace? [/h1]

[i]Orwell[/i] is a “visual novel” style game in which you have the ability to follow cyber-breadcrumbs in order to slowly uncover suspect’s online lives. Your goal? Stop a terrorist organization (?) from bombing public spaces. Your tools? As an agent, you are privy to the entirety of your target’s posts, articles, phone calls, emails, etc. Use this information to reveal more and more relevant webpages and conversations. The catch? You’re overlooked by a supervisor and you must choose what information to upload. This supervisor can only see the bits of information you feed him, so choose wisely or risk ruining an innocent’s life. The challenge? Upload only enough information to gain new leads, but not jump to conclusions. 

Are you really helping the greater good by invading the privacy of the few? Or have you caused more harm than good, muddling in affairs you should have never been in? Are the internet spies of today, really the superheroes of tomorrow? Find out by stepping into these large, cyber shoes. Act quickly and stop a harmful event in its tracks, or wait it out and discover it was a false alarm. Big brother is watching you. You are watching the people. Lives are on the line. Decide. 

Then watch as you say, [b]“I never meant for this to happen.”[/b]

Let me start off this review by saying I’m one who really enjoys a story-based game. I particularly enjoy consequence based story games (like [i]Telltale[/i]). If that’s not your cup of tea, this game is not for you. If you’re still interested, here’s the pros and cons for the game so far.

[h1]Pros:[/h1] [b]Interesting social commentary.[/b] There’s no denying that this is the age of technology, and with that comes a whole new slew of problems that our forefathers never could have foresaw when drafting the constitution. [i]Orwell[/i] heavily and obviously alludes to the current hot topics of freedom of internet access, government access to our personal files and correspondences, and general cyber security we see crop up in the news time and time again. 

[b]Easy interface.[/b] There’s not much to learn but drag and drop. Your un-uploaded data chunks are marked so you don’t lose track of what you’ve read, need to read, and are saving for later.

[b]More unique game flow.[/b] Events don’t happen unless you upload data chucks, leaving you to explore the branches of plot in whatever order feels natural to you. It does still feel a bit restricted, though, (see “A bit linear, limited” in cons) a perhaps more of a pseudo-free-directional choice. (But isn’t the concept of freedom what this game is all about?) 

[b]Intriguing artwork.[/b] The geometric artistic style lends itself to unconsciously nod its head towards the cyber-oriented world of the game. It ties in beautifully to the theme of the game—from the logo to the interface—without being too aggressive.

[h1]Cons:[/h1] [strike][b]A better save system!![/b][/strike] Update has added a rewind system, but I have not played since [strike]I cannot stress this enough. Since this is a consequence-based game, I’d like to be able to start from the end episode one, or so, with my decisions staying the same, and only make changes to my decisions from there out, with my profiles branching out from my first play through plot line. Starting over from the beginning is too much of a grind. Even a way to speed up messaging/call text on the second (and beyond) playthrough would be better for acheivement hunters or people just curious about the other endings. Examples of games with a good save system for this style of gameplay include [i]A Wolf Among Us[/i] and [i]Papers, Please.[/i][/strike]

[b]A bit linear, limited.[/b] There were some moments I wish some bit of text was highlighted (you may only drag and upload highlighted data chunks) since I wanted to explore that avenue of inquiry, but [i]Orwell[/i] had other plans. This gave the game a restricted feeling. It does not leave the game open to a world of naturally-occurring red herrings (only game-constructed ones, not user constructed), which I think would have added much more depth to the game. Also, it’s glaringly obvious which pieces of text carry great significance. (Those will be the ones with conflicting evidence) so sometimes the challenge of deciding to report information right away or wait was quite discernible, offering no challenge. Although, I will say that there are a few nuggets of data I uploaded without believing they would have as large of a consequence as they did. 

[b]Short.[/b] There’s only a little over forty minutes of game play per episode, and with five episodes, this leads to roughly four hours of gameplay (assuming you don’t replay events). I follow a rule of thumb of at least $1 to 1 hour of gameplay, so in that regard, it’s a bit pricey. Just wait for a sale. 

[h1]Remark:[/h1] [b]Play in one sitting[/b] (or as close to that as possible, if you don't have a full 4-5 hours to dedicate to one game) The flow and length of the game lends itself to be optimally played in one sitting. Taking a break and not have a comprehensive refresher (like the cinematic playbacks of key choices in [i]Telltale[/i] games) of your choices and actions is jarring to the enjoyment of the storyline in my opinion.

[h1]Conclusion:[/h1]
[b]I’d recommend buying [i]Orwell[/i] when on sale.[/b] It has an interesting and captivating storyline, despite some need of polishing. The interface, flow, and artwork lend itself to be an immersive experience into the lives of the people you are spying on to protect. Also, the current social commentary gives a real-world depth to the game. It does feel a bit restricting at times, and the story is short. The save system leaves much to be desired, since I would like to more easily explore all possibilities of my choices. But, despite these factors it was still enjoyable and fun to play.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
This is an incredible 'experience' of a game. Very immersive and gripping story right from the get go.

Characterisation is superbly done, with regular shifts in opinion of characters based on what they may or may not have done, new information comes to light constantly and you as the PC having to delicately manage your personal opinion against what is 'right' and meting out data that will in turn mete out justice.

To some of the other critics here, when looking at the gameplay elements:

There is often frustratingly insufficient evidence to go one way or the other on conflicting information - [i]That's the point[/i]. There's an allegory here for judicial systems of all stripes, that none have perfect information, even here in the information age.
And yes, sometimes you feel the need to submit certain pieces of evidence that aren't in line with the narrative you'd like to create order to progress - [i]That's the point[/i]. I felt conflicted and frustrated as a player of this [i]game[/i]. Imagine the confliction you would have in reality if you knew facts you provide would be wilfully misinterpreted by others to serve their own agenda? To be able to balance such a fine line of generating frustration in a player against the desire to see the story through to conclusion was masterful in my opinion.

A beautiful exploration of this very deep, philosophical point - that is matched by the aesthetic and depth of information to wade through in the game.

Bravo Surprise Attack Games - Orwell sets the bar in this 'cyperpunk storyteller' that will be difficult to surpass; and I'll definitely look forward to the 'datachunk' that you provide.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
[h1] George Orwell rolls in his grave [/h1]

Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You is an interactive novel exploring the increasingly popular notion that G. Orwell’s iconic “1984” ended up being a guideline for running a country, rather than a warning to its citizens. True to dystopian tones of its inspiration, the title opens up with a bombing attack on a public plaza. Several people were killed, perpetrators are unknown and public is in an uproar. This where you come in, as hand-picked investigator you will use the latest marvel of civil protection technology – Orwell, to solve the case. Orwell “the first and the last line of defence against terrorism” is a powerful software capable of accessing everything connected to the internet. Once a person is authorised by higher-ups for investigation, you are to upload any useful chunks of data into the software and Orwell will process them, granting you access to further information on the target. Person of interest has their phone number on their social media page? Now you can listen to their calls. An e-mail address published on their company’s website? Let’s take a peek inside. Is that a PC id number? You know the drill by now.

[b] Big brother stays vigilant [/b]
With power of Orwell at your fingertips, the player becomes breach of privacy incarnate, yet the decision whether to upload something or not is yours to make. At times you will have conflicting data, that may mislead the authorities acting upon your investigation, while certain details can be ignored altogether. On the other hand, there are also key data chunks that have to be uploaded in order to progress the story and, especially at early stages, there are not a lot of choices to make. Orwell is counterintuitive at first and software’s interpretation of data provided is downright puzzling at times. You better adapt to your new role quickly, as at certain junctions your choices will have an impact at the rest of the story.

It might have drawn your attention that I have addressed the title in question as an “interactive novel”, rather than a game. This is primarily due to the fact that aforementioned limited choice of data chunks thrown into the system is as far as gameplay goes. Alas, it is much easier to regard Orwell as a book, with webpages being equivalent of descriptions and eavesdropped calls and chats being the dialogues. Your investigation quickly unveils a hint of deeply-rooted conspiracy being at work and bombing is but a beginning of something much bigger. Plot divided into 5 chapters thickens quickly and while the general direction of the story is set in stone, your choices can greatly alter fate of certain characters and the ending is yours to twist.

[b] Blessed be the mind too small to question [/b]
Orwell is rather straight-forward with its thought-provoking intent. While the title’s plot unveils in delightfully ambiguous “The Nation”, it doesn’t take a particularly big leap of logic to start drawing parallels. Especially with themes of invigilation, media manipulation and a classic question of “whether the ends justify the means”. As with most of such questions and ideas, Orwell will be whatever you choose to make of it. It won’t be long though, as the title takes roughly 5 hours to complete, making it possible to finish Orwell in a single sitting. That said, the story is divided into coherent chapters of similar length, highlighted by the game as a good moment for a break, should you need one. Orwell is commendable for finding multiple sensible ways to underline impending conclusion of a plot thread, while staying reasonable from in-universe perspective.

Another facet of Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You, deserving a separate mention is the art style of the game. Admittedly, the opening cutscene fells remarkably clunky but everything past this very beginning is static images, allowing the style to truly shine. Every picture is built from colourful polygons giving the illustrations believable, yet somewhat obscured, feel to it. Much like the setting of the story, the visuals are deliberately vague, leaving making the parallels up to the player. 

When approached as a book, Orwell makes for enjoyable read with a highly unorthodox mode of delivery. I can easily recommend it to every fan of criminal thriller and political fiction as you should find yourself right at home. If one were to approach the title as a game though, there is very little to speak of. Should you also happen to be the type to skip dialogues in games as a habit, you should probably avoid Orwell like a plague.

P.S. Once you exit Orwell, you are greeted by advertisement of a sequel - Orwell: Ignorance is Strength. Fear not though, Keeping an Eye On You provides a complete storyline, no “to be continued” ending attached.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
If I could describe [i]Orwell[/i] in just two words, it would be "surprisingly smart". By that I mean: this is, obviously, a game about ubiquitous government surveillance, and that's not exactly a new theme. It would have been really easy to slap a "Big Brother BAD" plot on this, make it all about how you're one lone hero fighting the implacable government machine, give it a nice feel-good ending and be done with it. Or go the other way and go full grimdark with the boot stamping on a human face, forever. But [i]Orwell[/i] avoids taking the easy way out, and presents a very human story about how real people might act in a world where such a surveillance system exists. Sure, all the endings you can get (and there's a few) are still much more optimistic than George Orwell would be comfortable with, but hey, if you want [i]Nineteen Eighty-Four[/i], you know where to get it.

The gameplay is a simple affair where, in your role as a government agent, you look through available information (websites, chat transcripts, telephone calls) and collect relevant "data chunks", which in turn unlock more avenues for gathering information... and that's less boring than I'm making it sound, honest. For starters, it's not completely linear: sometimes the data you can collect is contradictory, irrelevant, or just plain wrong when taken out of context, and you have to apply your best judgement as to what goes in -- and the very fact that you're telling the system what to think of people based on the information you select comes back to haunt you in the story. Still, if you're looking for a puzzle game, or something that will challenge you beyond "did I forget to click on something somewhere", this isn't it. You're basically here for the story, but there's enough agency that you don't feel like you might as well have been reading a novel.

[i]Orwell[/i] isn't perfect. I got "stuck" once or twice when the game wanted me to put in some information I had deemed not worth uploading, or that I'd left to come back to later when I had more data -- the interface will track what you have and haven't seen, but not what you've seen but haven't acted upon. At these points (and some others) suspension of disbelief suffers a bit by the way the game artificially fences off information that, logically, should be available at any time. The graphics, while suitably stylized, are a bit [i]too[/i] stylized, especially when things need to animate. The music is fine (with some dramatic touches for when you've uncovered particularly dramatic info), but not remarkable. None of these things are deal breakers, though, and overall [i]Orwell[/i] is well worth its price tag as a solid, interactive story experience with an "It Could Happen Here!" theme that makes it that much more compelling.

review_text_clean: If I could describe [i]Orwell[/i] in just two words, it would be "surprisingly smart". By that I mean: this is, obviously, a game about ubiquitous government surveillance, and that's not exactly a new theme. It would have been really easy to slap a "Big Brother BAD" plot on this, make it all about how you're one lone hero fighting the implacable government machine, give it a nice feel-good ending and be done with it. Or go the other way and go full grimdark with the boot stamping on a human face, forever. But [i]Orwell[/i] avoids taking the easy way out, and presents a very human story about how real people might act in a world where such a surveillance system exists. Sure, all the endings you can get (and there's a few) are still much more optimistic than George Orwell would be comfortable with, but hey, if you want [i]Nineteen Eighty-Four[/i], you know where to get it. The gameplay is a simple affair where, in your role as a government agent, you look through available information (websites, chat transcripts, telephone calls) and collect relevant "data chunks", which in turn unlock more avenues for gathering information... and that's less boring than I'm making it sound, honest. For starters, it's not completely linear: sometimes the data you can collect is contradictory, irrelevant, or just plain wrong when taken out of context, and you have to apply your best judgement as to what goes in -- and the very fact that you're telling the system what to think of people based on the information you select comes back to haunt you in the story. Still, if you're looking for a puzzle game, or something that will challenge you beyond "did I forget to click on something somewhere", this isn't it. You're basically here for the story, but there's enough agency that you don't feel like you might as well have been reading a novel. [i]Orwell[/i] isn't perfect. I got "stuck" once or twice when the game wanted me to put in some information I had deemed not worth uploading, or that I'd left to come back to later when I had more data -- the interface will track what you have and haven't seen, but not what you've seen but haven't acted upon. At these points (and some others) suspension of disbelief suffers a bit by the way the game artificially fences off information that, logically, should be available at any time. The graphics, while suitably stylized, are a bit [i]too[/i] stylized, especially when things need to animate. The music is fine (with some dramatic touches for when you've uncovered particularly dramatic info), but not remarkable. None of these things are deal breakers, though, and overall [i]Orwell[/i] is well worth its price tag as a solid, interactive story experience with an "It Could Happen Here!" theme that makes it that much more compelling. review_text_raw:
Lately I've been finding myself bored with many games. I got through the motions without any real investment in what I've been playing... So, I decided to play something different. In comes Orwell. It's unlike any of the games I've toiled mundane hours hacking and slashing away in any random RPGs that I have on rotation. I've been engrossed in it for the past day getting familiar with the intricacies.

This is a different kind of spy game. One that might hit on reality a little closer than I'd like to think. Even more so if I was prone to ideas of the government watching our every move, which is why I'm an active VPN user. But I digress, Orwell is still just a game. A game where you play a data miner looking into the lives of who you might consider dangerous terrorists to a fictitious nation. I should mention there's quite a bit of reading. This isn't your mindless run and shoot game, or hide from the enemies and kill in secret game. It's not even graphically inspiring but the ideas and execution is solid. 

As you're uncovering terrorists and their plots you get deeper into the lives of those you think are involved and have to feed information into the Orwell system to determine their threat level. The game has you scouring through newspapers, blogs, and social media feeds to gain as much information as possible. It would be overwhelming if the interface wasn't so simple to navigate. 

While progression in the game is pretty linear you do have the ability to impact significant events based on what you choose to feed into the system. There is also an abundance of conflicting information that you will have to make judgement calls on what you want to submit. Orwell do a good job highlighting these inconsistencies. The only thing I might have qualms with is there's no "undo" feature. So if you do happen to make a mistake and upload something you'd rather not you don't have a second chance to fix or update your mistakes. The system for all it's abilities has a permanent function. Like most things once it's out there it's there for good. 

In all Orwell is an engaging game where you play big brother and stop terrorists a different way. It's got a solid story and characters and an easy to use interface. It may or may not resemble some truth to life but in the immortal words of Harold Finch "It's not paranoia if they really are out to get you" and in this game you're out to get everyone.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
A lightweight and interesting software title. "Orwell" is more of an interactive visual novel than a game, but tells a story well enough and the 2-4 hour playtime does not overstay too long. The plot is clear from the description and the marketing on Steam's storefront is accurate for what is offered - a tale of dystopia and hyper-surveillance where Your Choices Matter.

Much like "Papers, Please", there is a certain heroic conceit in an everyman investigator charting the path of the Nation, but the player will face real and weighty decisions with far-reaching consequences. By the mid-game, regular questions of guilt based on partial or contradictory evidence emerge and it will be up to you to decide what goes into the report and what does not. It can feel a little incomplete to mete out justice based on little more than social media posts and clipped messages from dubious surveillance, but I'll give a pass to the limited scope of the title because it is presented well and succeeds at reinforcing the message that privacy is complicated and imperfect.

The story also works well enough and there's some refreshing twists and dilemmas that keeps the plot intriguing so long as the player keeps up the tempo. I still feel like the later release of "Hypnospace Outlaw" is a better title in this game genre, but the commentary from "Orwell" about both security and authority are better storytelling than "Hypnospace" and does not disappoint. If you are like me then you'll only play it once and not again, but it's worth the $3 (USD) on sale to experience it and, if you're a fan of "1984", then this little simulation will fit you like a glove.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Conflict:  Orwell is an excellent game that is well designed and well written. 

Conflict: Orwell is a poorly written game that is horribly designed. 

Choose one. 

Orwell is a game that would demand someone choose one of these options, and the problem is is Orwell is an very good game, that is well written.  It however has some horrible design choices that stop me from calling it excellent or perfect.  In fact these design choices are VERY problematic. 


The entire game of Orwell is viewing webpages/conversations/phone calls and hunting down information and uploading it to a major database.  You're allowed free access to almost anything and you can upload almost anything to the database and play with it.  You'll get chastised for uploading garbage information, but it's also kind of fun.  Then the government who hired you to find the information will eventually operate on what you have found.   The story is told through these uploads and the results of your information gathering will change the story.  That's kind of cool. 

And Orwell tells a compelling (if a little predictable) story.  However it ends abruptly and seems to think it's ending can be a lot more impactful than it ends up being.   And then it falls into an egregious hole of pushing replayability but not allowing players to replay part of the story. 

But the thing is Orwell doesn’t really explain it’s gameplay.  The core of the gameplay is not what you upload, but rather what you choose not to upload, or how you choose to resolve conflicts.   But I really hate how it handles conflicts.  What it should do is allow you to upload conflicting information and have you choose how to resolve it explaining more “what do you think?”  Instead it makes this assumption that A or B is right and whichever you choose, they kind of operate on.  However that’s not how the world works, there’s conflicts in a single paragraph and the question is does the guy feel remorseful or does the guy feel responsible for the past… the answer is probably both, why make me choose. 

Then there’s other conflics that seem to not matter.  But what’s really important is what doesn’t get uploaded, and that’s kind of the problem. 

The first game you’re going to upload everything, because that’s what you think is right, but the game is VERY interesting when you don’t upload everything, you can change the game and the story minorly because of this.  You WILL end at the same point, but there is changes that happen. 

Sadly, the ending is a trinary Mass Effect style choice, that feels a bit eyerolling, even the “this ending is only unlocked if X” doesn’t happen and the end is really two or three screens.   I just want more interactivity in the story. 

The other problem is the final episode is actually excellent.  This is the episode where the game shines in a brand new way, it adds a new twist and limits the operator.  I almost wish this twist was added in day two or day three because it makes it much more intense to decide what you do, and I’d have liked to see the decisions on day 2 or 3 affect the ending, perhaps locking off the good ending if you fail. 

You see, the game feels a bit like the Teltale games, low interactivity, always reach the same ending and while that’s true, it’s not the same.  In Telltale, the same things happen no matter what, but in this game, there is changes, I just wish there was bigger meaningful changes that persisted, or even changed the ending and I’m hopeful for the future of Orwell because of that. 

But the story itself is good, if not as interactive as you like.  There’s good story twists, there’s good characters, and I actually like everyone involved in the story.  Orwell is supposed to be about the surveillance state, and even in that way Orwell shines.  And at 5 hours for a full gameplay it might seem expensive, but it can easily be played a second time.  

However replayability does suck, almost the entire game is the same and you have to play at least 3 or 4 hours to replay it.  I wish each episode would be replayable separate so I could go get the three endings of episode 3 and 5 without the full replay.  I didn’t mind a second replay but the third is abusive.

Overall though I DO like Orwell, the litmus test for this game is “did I put season 2 on my wish list” and I did.  I liked it that much.  10 bucks seems high but I think it’s worth the money, and even if not you can get it on sale.  It’s a unique experience, and a fun and interesting take on the surveillance state.  But even my complaint about the design and the way the game really presents it’s gameplay doesn’t ruin and interesting and engaging story. 

I’m hopeful, I want to see season 2 have more interactivity, I want to see season 2 involve more limitations on the user, and I want season 2 to be better, but for a first season of a rather novel game type, I’m pretty happy.  Orwell delivers what it intends to and I do adore how it does so.

review_text_raw:
'Orwell' is a fascinating first-person adventure game that explores the implications of online surveillance -- by having the player act as Big Brother! You play an investigator tasked with capturing perpetrators responsible for a lethal bombing. With the help of an investigative advisor, you collect Datachunks to build profiles of suspects.

However, profile building is not a rote task because you'll need to pore through online documents, phone and chat transcripts, resolve conflicting information, and be judicious and definitive about which Datachunk to add to the profiles. Given that, your decisions in building a suspect's profile will have both short-term and long-term consequences, affecting how the story unfolds. 

'Orwell' makes players reflect on, or perhaps even reconsider the value of and impact of surveillance on public safety. It's both entertaining and thought-provoking, and I was compelled to replay it twice more so that I can see how different decisions will yield different outcomes. With such high value in entertainment, intellectual stimulation and replayability for its price, 'Orwell' gets my enthusiastic recommendation.

review_text_raw:
This is a very interesting game, especially for anyone who has an interest in the surveillance state and the pros and cons of such a thing, mixed in with choices that really seem to matter.  I will admit that I have have, at the time of writing this review only played one playthrough, but the story was compelling and the information that I chose to put in/leave out really seemed to impact what was happening.  On top of that, the story is compelling, interesting and told through a very interesting way, feeding you snippets as you dig through the personal lives and media presence of several NPCs with various connections to one another, with a simple lock-off system that makes sense in-universe (we don't have clearance to investigate this person who has some connection to a potential suspect).

Beyond that, the only real issue I have with the game is the few interface bugs.  As the game went on, I found myself getting glitched to certain websites, mostly the [spoiler]work profile of the concerned one woman after she died in a shootout with law enforcement, and occasionally it would glitch to her dating profile.  This would normally happen when I was in either the listener or insider tools, seemingly never when I was on the reader tool already.  It would just switch me over as I tried to open a file on the insider, or load up into a machine, or even when I'd try opening a new conversation in the listener.[/spoiler]
One more slight drawback about the game is that sometimes you get told a bit too much by the game.  Game not letting you progress?  Something you thought was a lie was probably true.  Yellow highlight instead of blue?  You're going to get some information that conflicts with that.  I realise it would be a lot more work but a way to mark information as lies rather than just disabling it might help.  People don't always tell the truth and if you come to the conclusion that something true is a lie, it would be nice if the game didn't give away that you're wrong by just stopping time for you.  As for the other issue, it might be nice getting a window saying "Hey, this piece of information you're trying to add conflicts with this other information you've already added...which one do you think is true?", instead of just "Hey, at some point probably in the next 10 minutes you'll get another piece of information that will conflict with this here, we know that even though in-universe we haven't made the connection that that page with the conflicting information even exists!"

All in all a really great game with a simple premise, easy to learn with some fairly minor flaws that can honestly be overlooked most of the time.

Pros:
+ Loved the artwork of the game

review_text_raw:
[h1]A fun little game with a few annoyances.[/h1]
[i]Review correct as of episode 2[/i]


Orwell plays its premise on its sleeve, but that's not a bad thing. Orwell's a lovely modern take on the dystopian Orwellian society from 1984, where surveillance is king and social media reveals your darkest secrets. The ruling government of your fictional country; rather menacingly known as, 'The Party'; is toned down to a believable level, less thought police coming to take those whom merely forget the government's new lie; more observing and taking people who know more than they think for a quick chat... In a windowless cell...

You play a new agent to an experimental scheme, brought about by their version of the patriot act, who spys on its people to counter terrorist acts. Unfortunately, you've come at a bad time, there's been a dramatic terrorist bombing and you've got to find those reponsible. Luckily, deus ex machina, you've been directed to a person of interest whom happens to be very weakly linked to the terrorist/s. Better start investigating. 

Investigations are done by exploring a person's current and past life in detail and it's a fun little bit of gameplay. You simply open either a website or a report and the, "government's advanced computers", scan the page for anything it thinks relevant to the investigation. It's up to you to decide what to include in your report by dragging and dropping highlighted items onto said report. Sadly, Osmotic Studios has decided that you can't change anything you drag onto your report. Accidentally mistake a bit of text saying they live in Wonderland as information on their mental instability rather than what the game has decided, which is that they physically live in Wonderland? Well tough titties, you can't change that. 

At times the game does spice things up with multiple choice moments. Throughout the game, contradictory information will be presented to you and it's up to you to decide which is the correct bit of information. But! But! There isn't always an obvious answer! Which infuriates a few people. But it shouldn't. People who get frustrated are sadly missing the obvious answer the game's trying to present to you. The truth doesn't matter. You are the truth. What you decide can and will be the truth. You pick the option which suits your needs, think person A is a dissdent to 'The Party'? Then the correct answer is that the man is a dissdent. No matter what contradictory information you see. This is the beauty of Orwell and this is were the game really shines. Sometimes though these options are forced. Two bits of information are in fact the same piece of information just it's presented in a way to force a choice, when in reality you could easily push both those pieces in a well worded report.

While the gameplay is enjoyable, where Orwell really shines is in it's narrative. The characters you are investigating are nicely fleshed out and you can get a real sense of who that person is and that's an important factor in a game like this. No matter how good a story you have, if the people you are investigating are dull or unbelievable it could really ruin a game like this, gladly I can say this hasn't happened. While it is rather short it has a nice progression and you can feel the underlying sense a deeper plot and the frustrating feeling of grasping at the strings of truth. A feeling further emphasised by the episodic nature of the game, gladly the timeframe is rather short and the feeling is rather than them having a product that isn't complete, they're trying to tailor the story from the fans suggestions and mood.

There weren't many things I disliked about Orwell. My biggest gripe is almost a personal choice, I've already mentioned a few smaller issues already such as forced choices and the fact information placed into the report cannot be edited, but I think Orwell misses a beat when it comes to power of the government. It wants to present a Orwellian society for the modern day and tries to do this by suggesting your powers and the government's powers are legally limited at certain moments. This is personally the opposite way I wish they had gone. For starters modern goverments have incredible powers just have a gander at the Patriot Act (US),  the 2000/2006 terrorism act (GB), and états d'urgence - constitution of 1958 (Fr). I wish Orwell had taken this and gone further, showing a government whose powers were even more unfettered.

In summation I rather like Orwell and it's a game I can very heartily recommend to anyone who would like a nice story driven narrative, and can get through the rather lengthy bits of text one has to read. There are some personal gripes I have with the story but overall nothing that you would really be a deal breaker.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Orwell stars you, the player, as an investigator in the Nation's (a stand-in for an unholy almagamation of the United States and the United Kingdom) new, government-ordained spying programme. Your job is to investigate suspected terrorists and cherrypick data you've acquired via researching the Internet and spying directly on their conversations, phones, and computers. You upload these data modules to the Orwell database and help construct a profile of these suspects that your advisor (who can't see your research sources in an effort to maintain some sort of ethical loophole) then uses to report back to the authorities, thus causing your actions to have potentially devastating consequences.

I've seen a few people complain about the gameplay--you are, essentially, dragging these data modules from one part of your screen to another (and, frustratingly, it can take a few clicks to get hold of them), which sounds unexciting on paper. But the story is compelling, and it's through this (slightly repetitive and boring) gameplay that you unlock the story, which can branch depending on which data you upload to Orwell. Some of it you have to, some of it you don't--and some of it you can use to alter the perception of certain suspects by picking which element of contradicting data you want to show to the advisor. 

The game does a very good job of highlighting how people become complacent with this level of privacy invasion--I've seen complaints of the game handholding you throughout, but, in my opinion, this helps you to slip into the mindset of uploading whatever data you come across, mindlessly painting suspects as victims because it's what your advisor wants of you. It wasn't until the end of my first playthrough that I realised how much damage I'd caused by providing evidence to suggest that innocent people were guilty of crimes they hadn't committed, and how many of the characters I'd either had arrested or killed via my actions of "innocuously" collecting their data. Which I guess is what the game wants you to do, particularly on a first playthrough.

That's not to say I don't have complaints. The game wants you to play multiple playthroughs, even if only to collect all of the achievements (most of which can be acquired in two playthroughs; two require a third, or replaying chapters on one of your profiles). Different actions have different outcomes and dialogue, and that produces slightly new scenes to watch (or, really, read). The problem is that the texts and calls you have to monitor can be so tediously long, particularly with little deviation--the last chapter has one that's just about shy of 10 minutes, and you can't do anything but sit and let it play. There's no option to skip the scene. 

I've also seen a few people complain that the game thinks people can never lie or exaggerate, which I assume refers to options where you can report suspects for having outspoken anti-government tendencies... but again, I think this is overlooking what the game wants you to consider. 

I highly recommend Orwell, although I bought it in the Humble Bundle and so bought it for much cheaper than its standard price--and I've already collected all the achievements in just over 6 hours of play, which isn't quite a £1 = 1 hour of playtime at its normal price. It's obviously not a game that's appealing to everyone, but I do think for those that like immersive visual novels with political themes (and that's essentially what it is), you'll enjoy Orwell.

review_text_raw:
Wow I am more than impressed with this game. I am a big fan of the game genre of "Papers, Please", "This is the police" and similar games. I think when games explore your morals and hits you right in your cognitive dissonance. This game does this incredibly well. Surveilence is a difficult subject. There are pros and cons that vary between people.

This game sets your objective as having you aid in finding the suspect for a terrorist attack. This is of course a justifiable action and is in good favor for the public. You quickly start having conflicting thoughts about whether the people you're spying on and the information you gather is relevant at all. I am the type of person who is really interested in other people's affairs. This game absolutely worked wonders on this quirk of mine because I found it difficult to resist to look deeper in people's personal lives. I bet you will too constantly convince yourself that "this guy's past relationship drama might prove useful later".

The writing in this game is absolutely amazing in my honest opinion. This game felt real. The information layout, news articles, blogs, emails, texts, calls all felt real. The way you quickly progress from getting basic information on one person such as their name and occupation suddenly turns into having direct sneaky access to their desktop files, bank account activity and search history. You will find a lot of surprises in this game and lots of VERY difficult choices. There is a lot of conflicting ideas this game forces on you. For example you are presented with 2 or 3 very contradicting pieces of information. Sometimes it is easy to choose based on the source of where this info came from but when the consequences are severe, you are under pressure to make the right choice as there is no going back.

One downfall of this game is that there are some slight errors in the scripting that messes up the flow. For example there are certain bits which I suppose are meant to be discovered in a certain sequence but its possible to do it in the wrong sequence, resulting in dialogue that doesn't fit in. Alerting the higher ups of a threat after it already happened results in them thanking you for the useful information and that they will be prepared...even though this happened just recently and they were not prepared. The game also decides on itself which information is relevant or not and kind of makes you feel bad for collecting everything you might feel is necessary but thankfully you are not outright punished for it. Another big error I noticed was with relationships. I find out that a character has been married in the past and add it to the database but the database instead labels the character as currently married which is considered as wrong information until you find out more details later.

All in all these negatives do not affect the game much. This game is worth full price and I think is a must buy with a discount.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
This a pretty clever little narrative game. 

You essentially play the role of an investigator using a survelliance software system called Orwell, and investigate people that are citizens of a country referred to as "The Nation", that seems to be modeled off of present day Western nations like the US, UK, Canada etc. You don't have total access to everything, as your adviser often needs to 'get clearance' to add someone to the target list, but you still wield a chilling amount of investigative power eventually. 

This is not set in an extreme totalitarian world like the state of Oceania in [i]1984[/i], but a mostly present day world. It's a bit ambiguous though, as a couple real countries are referred to eventually, and 'The Nation' has some ominous things about it that suggest a veiled totalitarianism, especially with references to 'The Party'.  

There isn't alot of 'gameplay' to it, as you basically just use the mouse to collect bits of information on people from your various electronic sources. It's UI is basically the same ideas as using a computer and web browser.  

While all selectable information is highlighted for you, you do have to make decisions about what information to upload to a person's Orwell profile, and that can have major consequences for events in the story.  Some info is obviously useful, some is just mundane, some bits of info conflict with others. With the conflicting info though, i wish there were sometimes more avaliable info to make a better judgement, but I guess that's the point. 

There are at least a few different endings, but you may have to do a full playthrough again to get them, i'm not sure. 

Without giving away any spoilers to the story, there is a persistent (and i'm sure intentional) irony about the people you are tasked to investigate.  The in-game stated purpose of Orwell and your position is to protect the nation from terrorist threats.  The story starts off when a small bomb goes off in Freedom Plaza.  From that point, the network of people you investigate are all tied to the ideology of wanting privacy. Basically, you are doing the exact things that are fueling this ideology. 

This is excellent social and political commentary in the form of a simple game, and I would definitetly recommend it!

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
[b]tl;dr:[/b] The description doesn't make clear that this is a visual novel. Don't expect much decision making, or even actual deduction--[i]Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You[/i] holds your hand throughout the experience. If you can forgive that, and stomach the occasionally doubleplusungood prose, you'll have a decent (if predictable) exploration of surveillance. Modestly recommended; only buy during sales.

-

It's the World Of Tomorrow™, and an enigmatic nation known only as, well, The Nation is preparing the implementation of an as of yet unannounced surveillance program. With the Orwell AI on your side, you are tasked with finding the culprit of a terrorist attack, so that the government can prove the efficacy of the program and rally the support of the public. But things are not as they seem, and what was supposed to be a simple case quickly spirals out of control.

Actual gameplay, if it can be called that, mostly consists of diving into the digital lives of target persons. Now and then, the AI will highlight processable pieces of information, which are known as datachunks. If you feed a datachunk to the system, it will be sent to a government advisor on the other end of the line, who can then use the evidence to justify an arrest, call in a special ops team, et cetera. Because the advisor only gets to see those datachunks that you choose to process, he can't really read the information in its proper context, allowing you to paint a misleading picture through selectivity. By (ab)using this indirect influence, you can steer the turn of events into your preferred direction.

The idea sounds interesting enough on paper, and admittedly, it sometimes is--when the game is at its best, your choices really [i]do[/i] feel as if they matter. More often than not, though, you just go down a funnel, with your advisor telling you what to do for every step of the way. Events are supposed to happen in real-time, but are actually tied to your storyline progress; after something significant has happened, events will usually grind to a halt until you've passed some checkpoint. This implementation strips the concept of much of its strength, and it would be nice if Osmotic Studios had been a tad bit more honest about this. Indeed, I went in with a much more sandboxy expectation. Buyer, beware: [i]Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You[/i] is a glorified visual novel, with no real interaction beyond some scripted points of divergence. I don't think that is necessarily a bad thing. I [i]do[/i] think it is important to know.

Another thing that cheapens the experience is the implausible interface of the AI. From time to time, you will encounter two contradictory datachunks, but instead of doing the sensible thing (uploading them both for later review), the AI will [i]force[/i] you to make a choice, even if you don't have nearly enough context to do so informedly. For some reason, these uploads can't be reversed if you find better information down the road. Even more questionably, the AI can somehow [i]know[/i] that a certain datachunk will contradict with another, even if the contradicting datachunk hasn't been found yet! I understand that these things are necessary for gameplay purposes--calling the shots in solving contradictions is one of the key ways to manipulate your advisor--but they really do shatter one's immersion.

So far, I have been pretty negative about this game, so you might be wondering why I still recommend it. The reason is quite simple: the story, is well worth experiencing. Characters feel like real, actual people who could be living next door, not like empty robots who are just there to advance the plot. And it is the very lack of meaningful choice that allowed the writers to go this far: most games are wide but shallow, [i]Orwell[/i] is narrow but deep. Granted, the attempts to make the player question their own morality mostly fall flat (contrary to what the reviewer consensus seems to be, good and evil are clear from the start), and the social commentary that permeates the writing has a distinct feeling of 'heard it all before'. There is also an overreliance on deus ex machina, particularly near the end of the story. But the characters and their various interactions are captivating enough to make you genuinely care about their fates. You might even find yourself on the edge of your seat, even though you never get to see the action directly. In my opinion, that more than makes up for the cheap plot devices, as well as the [i]very[/i] variable quality of the prose. The many references to George Orwell's [i]Nineteen Eighty-Four[/i] add to the charm.

In short, [i]Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You[/i] is a mediocre game, but with a respectable narrative. As long as you keep your expectations in check, it will certainly provide an afternoon of entertainment.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
[h1]A memorable and engaging experience.[/h1]

Orwell puts you in the shoes of an investigator working for a police state. The goal is to identify and build a case against suspected terrorists using both publicly available and personal/confidential information. Information you upload enables access to further sources. Uploading mention of a notable injury will unlock access to the person's medical records; finding a phone number or email lets you spy in on their correspondence etc. 

But information you upload could be incorrect, or misinterpreted/twisted to suit the government's agenda. How far will you go? Who will you condemn?

[h1]How is it?[/h1]

This core is compelling and unique enough to carry the game through to its conclusion. The comparisons to Papers Please are obvious, but Orwell is far more expansive. Where Papers Please created tension by pitting you against a time limit, Orwell creates a complex, intriguing and politically relevant narrative where you never truly know who is or isn't guilty. It is hard to discuss in detail without spoiling, but the story is full of twists and turns and finds a way to successfully play out dramatic scenes that you experience from behind the safety of your computer screen and the shield of Orwell.

The soundtrack compliments the game nicely, and is used effectively to punctuate important revelations in the story.

It's entirely text-based, and game length depends entirely on your reading speed and habits. Speed-reading and scanning for pertinent information (which the game highlights for you) can shorten the game to 3-4 hours. A more thorough and careful reading, especially if read aloud, can extend your playtime to 8 hours. The game will be a one-time experience for most players, but the game lets you play each episode individually once cleared, and there's enough agency in what optional & conflicting information you upload that replayability is there for those that want it.

[h1]However[/h1]

The game has enough flaws to feel like it wasn't thoroughly tested.

Conflicting information is highlighted in yellow, rather than blue. You can only upload one of these, so the game highlights conflicting information before you've identified what it conflicts with. This is both a minor spoiler and very awkward, and could have easily been handled better.

It's easy to get overwhelmed with information. The game highlights sources with new information for you, but distinguishing between what is optional and mandatory to upload is not obvious. Perhaps this is intentional, but it is too easy to be stuck in a deadlock with 30 possible sources to go through trying to find the one piece of mandatory information you refrained from uploading the first time. An additional icon highlighting old sources with uploadable information would have made this much less tedious.

Spying in on peoples phone conversations happens in real time. This has a wonderful voyeuristic feel to it, but the conversations progress far too fast to read aloud at a comfortable speaking pace. This would be fine if they didn't contain time-sensitive information that needs to be uploaded during the conversation itself. Anyone streaming this or reading aloud to themselves will be caught in the awkward spot of either missing the window to upload information, or have to voice act far too fast for the conversation to sound natural.

Finally, the writing itself is simply poor. I wonder if it was written by a native English speaker or a trained writer. The grammar is awkward, misleading or just incorrect far too often, and this does detract from the otherwise believable world and engaging story the game creates. Simple proof-reading would have solved this.

None of these are game-breaking or significantly ruin the game, but all are so needless, so simply and easily solved that their inclusions are frustrating.

[h1]Verdict[/h1]

If you liked Papers Please, find the theme compelling or want a unique text-based game, you'll enjoy this. It comes with too many niggling issues to recommend at full price, but with a small discount this will be a worthwhile experience that will stay with you for years to come.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Finished in 3 hours, did not replay to look for alternate choices.

You play as a character who works for the government and has complete access to internet, phone calls, text messages, etc. Your job is to investigate people, collect evidence, and solve (and prevent) terrorist crimes. You're the man behind the camera in the all-seeing surveillance state. 

The way the surveillance system is set up is that you collect the information and pass it to an analyst. The analyst looks at the information and decides whether it is sufficient to arrest somebody, or enough to indicate another person is a person of interest that you're allowed to investigate. Over time the network of people you're investigating grows, and it's harder to keep track of their history and relationionships.

If you collect the correct information, you might be able to prevent terrorist attacks. It is possible to get enough evidence to arrest people who aren't actually dangerous or ringleaders.

Sometimes, you see conflicting information (such as when one person is lying) and you need to make a decision. You can't submit both pieces of evidence, you can't delete evidence once you've submitted it (silly, but a game mechanic to make your choices more meaningful), and sometimes it's not clear which one is correct. You sometimes can dig around and find out which piece is correct, but sometimes you need to go with your gut and what you think the people's motivations are. 

Other times, it's not clear that you're making a choice. You can always choose to submit or not submit information, and it could lead to different results. The only way to know this is to replay the game and deliberately not choose things that led to bad outcomes. At first I was just grabbing and submitting all the information I saw, but you're intended to put a bit more thought into it. Is this relevent information? Do you want the analyist making a decision based on this information? Is this quote being taken out of context? Are you encouraging your analyist to arrest a harmless person?

My only complaint about the game is [spoiler] there is only one case/group you get to investigate, and that investigation turns "meta" at the end -- having discovered the ORWELL system you're using to spy on them, they start interacting with you directly. I kind of wanted to see the system working as intended for a few cases before the "finale" case where your subjects figure out what's going on.[/spoiler] I know it's a smaller indie type of game, but a few more cases to establish what you're doing, how significant your choices are, and so on BEFORE it reached that point would have been appreciated.

I did enjoy this game. It involves a lot of reading, and a lot of thinking, in order to enjoy it properly. It's not a good game for people who want to click through the boring stuff to get to the exciting part. In a way, it's more akin to the visual novel genre than it is to more traditional games.
