game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Sometimes the best story games are the simplest ones...

A simple yet effective game on Osmotic Studios' part, Orwell introduces the player to a world featuring all the thematic faculties of its namesakes' original novel. Through only a computer screen, the player views much this populated universe through such a small window in its beautiful geometric collage art style. In a nation that spies on its citizens in the name of public safety and security, the player must make choices that directly impact the narrative, potentially leading to the suspects' fates in questionable circumstances. With Orwell, truth becomes fickle and fact becomes fiction as information the player chooses to upload draws parallels towards that same old novel. Additionally, with the suspects' profiles altered however the player sees fit, this game brings about a fair amount of replay-ability as the fate of the Nation is revealed by the players handiwork.

My only critique is how easily the story is driven through click and dragging of information that immediately becomes visible once the player scrolls through it. This choice in development diminishes some of the challenge in finding the facts through all the media debris. While I understand the developers chose the feature to avoid breaking their game, I believe having to read the actual articles and having more conflicting data to choose from would have made this game more enthralling.

8/10! I'm keeping my eye on you too!

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
I've always been one to read all of the books/letters/e-mails in games, but they rarely do more than build the world or give character backstory. I also tend to agonize over decisions in dialogue trees, worried that the "wrong" answer will cut me off from more interesting story lines. Orwell is a game that completely commits to reading and interpreting as the primary game mechanics. It succeeds at telling a satisfying story, even if it sometimes trips on the complexities of these mechanics as storytelling tools.

There are issues: The interface isn't as robust as you would hope. For instance, you can drag pictures of people from the Web into their profile, but only certain ones. At one point I found pictures of two new "persons of interest" on their corporation's website, but I couldn't drag their photos into their profiles. The game also runs into the issue that we have expectations of what can be done on the Internet. For instance, when you get the ability to break into someone's phone and can see where they've been, you expect that the addresses will tell you what is actually at those locations, but Orwell doesn't tell you this, you have to either remember or infer what is there.  

You can also get trapped when the story tries to funnel you to a certain plot point. In one part of the game there was nothing for me to do but to choose between two pieces of conflicting information: Which of two people organized a protest? The problem is that there was no way for me to make that call, it was pure he said/she said. I had a hunch, but it wasn't backed by any concrete information, and given what I had come to realize was the black-and-white nature of the Orwell system, I wanted to have something concrete before making this decision. Unfortunately, in order to progress the story I was forced to make the call based on nothing more than a hunch. 

And sometimes it seems like you need to make the wrong choice when one set of conflicting information would clearly open up a whole new tangent and the conflicting data wouldn't, so you choose the first even though you know the second is just as likely to be correct. For instance, at one point a character was accused of being gay, but there was conflicting information that he actually had a wife and kids. Of course, these two things don't conflict at all, there are plenty of gay people who have been in heterosexual relationships and even marriages. In fact, this character left his wife and children and the accusation that he was gay came many years later, so clearly one could argue that he left his wife and family BECAUSE he was gay. But in order to progress the story and open up profiles on the wife and learn more about that part of his life, I had to choose the wife data over the gay data. 

Sometimes the AI just breaks, especially that of your handler, Symes. For instance, one time I added the info that a certain character had a new girlfriend, that he wasn't with his old girlfriend, Juliet. Symes chimed in that he never knew that this character and Juliet were a couple, but I had put that information in both of their profiles a long time ago. And sometimes Symes is just clueless: At one point we discovered the name of a new character, one for whom we previously only knew her online handles, and he said something like "So she's been hiding her real name, eh?" Of course she was! Who always uses their real name for their online accounts?

It seems that there are probably multiple endings, but I only played it through once. There are no manual saves, so to get other endings you would have to play through the whole game again, which I'm not interested in doing. I wasn't entirely satisfied with my ending, but I still think that the journey was compelling and timely, probably more timely than the developers even realized when they started working on it. Orwell is a fascinating experience, especially if you are at all interested in our current information culture and the balance between government data gathering and personal privacy.

For instance, one time I added the info that a certain character had a new girlfriend, that he wasn't with his old girlfriend, Juliet. Symes chimed in that he never knew that this character and Juliet were a couple, but I had put that information in both of their profiles a long time ago. And sometimes Symes is just clueless: At one point we discovered the name of a new character, one for whom we previously only knew her online handles, and he said something like "So she's been hiding her real name, eh?" Of course she was! Who always uses their real name for their online accounts? It seems that there are probably multiple endings, but I only played it through once. There are no manual saves, so to get other endings you would have to play through the whole game again, which I'm not interested in doing. I wasn't entirely satisfied with my ending, but I still think that the journey was compelling and timely, probably more timely than the developers even realized when they started working on it. Orwell is a fascinating experience, especially if you are at all interested in our current information culture and the balance between government data gathering and personal privacy.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Orwell is, as you might guess from the title, a near-future dystopian terrorism thriller told through the lens of the titular national surveillance system of a fictional country called simply The Nation. You learn about the characters through their chat logs, social media and blog posts etcetera and slowly build up a picture of what is going on. But will it be the right picture, or will it lead to more bombings? Will the guilty parties get arrested or will law enforcement focus on the wrong targets? All this and more is up to you, as a faceless "investigator" assigned to the Orwell mass surveillance project.

It looks like it was originally released episodically but it works just as well playing it all the way through. But remember: the system only makes connections based on the data YOU upload to it. If you pick the wrong information, things can go sideways very badly.

I picked this game up in the Christmas 2016 sale and have enjoyed my first playthrough greatly, so I highly recommend it for anyone looking for a story and character driven thriller of this kind. Do be prepared for a lot of clicking, scrolling and dragging and dropping though.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
What is Orwell ?

Orwell is a game that has managed to make me fully immersed into it, which is something rare, whenever a game makes me Immersed, it automatically makes that game good for me. In concept orwell introduces you into a terrorist situation and you are an hired investigator who must use this new tool called "Orwell" to bring justice to the people involved in this specific situation, the gameplay is very simple, its just clicking and dragging stuff on screen but I'd rather play this and be immersed than play the latest AAA release and fall asleep just 2 hours in, what makes Orwell special is that its a game that every single choice matter, nothing is black and white, for every stuff you do during your investigation, the special traits the supposed terrorist have that you highlight on their profile, to the locations they visited, their personal lives and the people they have a relationship with, all the occurrences that happen during the 5 days the game takes place on, whenever you finish one of the five chapters aka complete a day of investigations theres a lot of consequences, good or not based on what you decided to highlight, since Orwell itself as a program has a imbued browser system and a profile you have to search every corner for information and make sure that youre putting the correct person in jail, theres contradicting information, I for example failed hard on the second day of investigations, I sent the police to the wrong location and because of that a bomb exploded in a public area, killing innocents, something I could prevent and by the end of the game, no matter what you do, we both will always get different endings since theres so many variables at stake and Orwell is such a detailed and immersive game, it makes every decision count. Another thing to add is that the game plays into hard topics that are relevant to our current times and the game does it in such smart way, its not just another pretentious game, its a smart, well-done game. 

Besides the concept Orwell presents a nice soundtrack and a great sense of style, you will always be looking into this program for most of the time but the game uses this environment to show its great artistic design and despite the gameplay being overly simple with the complex way your decisions are taken into consideration, the immersion the game pulls you into and the very interesting way that this game story which Imo was really well done develops, it just becomes a seamless experience, it took me 5 hours to finish and I would gladly replay it again and this time correcting the mistakes I did on my previous playthrough, I think that Orwell is simple an indie masterpiece, it executes its concept with class, add interesting takes into the whole cybersecurity concept and has a simple but engaging gameplay, In my opinion if you want to try something different that stays with you then this game is a must-play, a very memorable and original game.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Okay first off, I just finished the game for the first time through, so I can only speak to the progression of the game through my single experience. 

What an entangled, involved, deep ride it was! All the minor and major bits of plot and character development... left me speechless. When I first got into this game, I was hopeful that it wouldn't be a flimsy investigative journalism style that left gaping holes in character development in favor of quick story progression. So with endless red herrings, conflicting information, tiny bites (bytes?) of data that all weave together, I very quickly became engrossed in finding out everything I could, and frequently found myself at odds with my own judgments and thoughts based on what the information was telling me. 

The atmosphere of the game is sober, at times haunting, and at times pulse quickening depending on what's going on. And I think that this is very much appropriate for the moral of the story. This is invasive, what the player is forced to do... to get this job done. It spends time and effort bringing the player from one side of the spectrum to the other in terms of how helpful or hurtful a surveillance system like Orwell can be. 

In the end, or at least the end of the story I found... I was left with a feeling of completion... ... and thoughtfullness. Yes it's a game, but it has a very real moral message in it, that when the end credits roll make you really consider the implications of our REAL digital lives, and how easy it is to comb through and assemble these very damning dossiers. And how dangerous that could be if the 'powers' that be decided to use it as a means of control and 'protection'. I haven't reacted to a game in this way in a long time... so it bears a review. 

Extremely well made, thought provoking, in depth, orwellian (aptly named!), driving, robust game WELL worth a play. The only drawback I can find is that some people don't like a game where they have to read a lot. And there's a TON to read, combing through all the various resources for hints and clues, and entanglements.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
This game proves that you dont need fancy graphics for an immersive gaming experience. 

Orwell forces you to rethink the ideas of government, control, surveilance and the right to go : FK YOU; all presented inside the framework of the paranoid dystopian world originally created by George Orwell back in 1948.

Orwell, however is a modern, slick version of Oceania, in which you play a state agent gathering information on citizens in a world that is under perpetual surveilance.  Your role is to select relevant data bites to pass onto a computer system  designed to identify potential threats to the Nation's status quo. 

Where 1984 is a distant dystopia that can likened to far off places like North Korea,  the world of Orwell is far more like the very one we live in. Where the state operatus of Oceania is something that is menacing, power hungry and paranoid, the shades of powerplay in this world is deceptively bright, fresh and friendly, yet equally suspicious and potentially sinister. 

As you gather information you become acutely aware of your own actions and how they potentially affect the lives of the citizens you scrutinize, as you decide which bytes of information will be passed on and which will be hidden.  There are occasions where you will find contradictory information, presenting opposing beliefs, yet easily accepting the vailidy of both in your mind simultaneously.  However, unlike reading Orwell, and having the answers written out for you, here you are  co-conspirator in Big Brother. You start to question the ideas around good and  evil and discover things that potentially, are both.

The concept of the game is as fascinating as the mind games you start playing with yourself as you potentially prosecute or persecute citizens in a world where freedom and control are at constant odds with one another. 

There are more episodes to come,  and the final verdict will not be out for a while, but so far it is a unique and intriguing experience. Possibly the most rewarding asect about the game, is not the game itself, but the things you start to question, even when not playing the game. Though the brilliance of 1984 is in a league all by itself, there is no doubt that this games manages to bring the message in a far more suble way, and succeed in making it relevant to the world we live in today.

That in itself makes for unique and rewarding gameplay, and it would not be outrageous to suggest that Orwell breaks new ground  in the story/novel game genre.

On the flipside, the game is a little too easy, too much handholding and very linear, and the excecution, though good, could have been a lot better. 

HIghly recommended if you are an Orwell fan, even more so if you know little or nothing about 1984.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
I don't know how I came across the game, I had never heard of it until last week. I'm very familiar with George Orwell's 1984 so when I saw this game randomly I thought hell ya.

The gameplay is a bit like the old hacker's game "Uplink". Simple GUI that you, the "user" sit's behind a virtual system to do your work. 

Gameplay: It may seem like you have to do a lot of reading but this "Orwell" system tends to pick out what it thinks is important and relevant information. It's up to you to deem it important. If it is important, it'll unlock new stuff for you to read and so forth. At times you'll get conflicting information, this is the best part of the game as you have to decide, based on the profile you built on the person, which piece of information fits the puzzle.

You can read deeper into emails if you want, it makes you feel more part of the story and the world but you can also skim quite a bit, you'll just miss out on feeling like you know these people, without actually meeting them, it's a little creepy.

Story: It's great. At first I was a little detached from it because I didn't know if a game like this was going to be able to have a deep story. It does. It's told through emails, text messages, phone calls etc.

Took me 6 hours to complete and I don't feel a single one of those minutes was a waste.

The art style was great. I loved the polygon look while still being detailed.

Interface is super easy to use, they did a really good job on this.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
[h1] "For The Nation, for the security of the citizens, for their safety, I shall be the investigator. The one who shall observe and... eliminate." [/h1]

What is in this mysterious name: Orwell? A good plot? Realism and coherence? A branching storyline? Memorable characters? Plot twists? Perhaps, all of the mentioned and a lot more? Yes - all of the mentioned and A LOT more. This game is a very interesting game in which you'll act as an investigator working for a governmental project called "Orwell." With the help of this mass surveillance software/tool, you will be tracking and evaluating various people to identify potential "threats" to The Nation. The evaluation process includes analyzing social media accounts of the people evaluated, their chat histories, emails, phone calls, personal devices, and etc. Basically anything, which they deemed a part of their "private" life. 

What I really liked about this game is its attention to detail. On the first look, the game's storyline contains lots of unnecessary snippets of information, which might be regarded as useless by the inattentive player. However, those little details and discrepancies form a larger picture which reveals a major plot twist that takes place somewhere in the ending episodes. The plot twist itself [spoiler], which was about Juliet being the imposter instead of the suspected Harrison,[/spoiler]did make sense after some other playthroughs (accomplishing all the achievements and endings) as I've paid a lot of attention to those little details in the game. [spoiler]For me, the hint provided by Symes about Juliet's favorite book (The Mockingbird)and Harrison's lost phone seemed like the ones which can directly lead you towards the "Juliet is the true imposter" conclusion. [/spoiler]Well, the game proved to me that no story can be regarded as completely explored without the consideration of all the small details. A lesson well learnt.

As much as I liked this game, there are still things that can be improved. For instance, adding a setting for an accelerated playthrough, because DAMN, some of the calls take more than 10 minutes to finish and are unskippable. Going through the game again becomes a real pain without this feature. I understand that some events happen during phone calls (which is probably why you can't accelerate them), but as a person who finished the main plot multiple times, I don't bother to read all the stuff again. Besides, I think players decide beforehand their choices, so adding the accelerated playthrough won't hurt the experience much (it is wise to lock it until the game is completed for the first time). There were some spelling (Episode 3; objective; "motiviation") and grammar mistakes, but those are minor issues. Apart from these, there aren't much things which I'd want to be added to this game. 

I've written too much for this review already and thus will conclude my overall impression for the game. The game is truly amazing BUT is not for everyone. If you crave for action and excitement and don't like reading and analyzing, then I do not recommend this game to you. But hey! It's never a bad time to explore a new frontier and discover a little bit more about yourself. Maybe you'll love this game the same as I did and give it a thumbs up. 

[u]-QG7 Recommended[/u]

There were some spelling (Episode 3; objective; "motiviation") and grammar mistakes, but those are minor issues. Apart from these, there aren't much things which I'd want to be added to this game. I've written too much for this review already and thus will conclude my overall impression for the game. The game is truly amazing BUT is not for everyone. If you crave for action and excitement and don't like reading and analyzing, then I do not recommend this game to you. But hey! It's never a bad time to explore a new frontier and discover a little bit more about yourself. Maybe you'll love this game the same as I did and give it a thumbs up. [u]-QG7 Recommended[/u]

Although it has its flaws (a few times I was frustrated that some data chunks were "contradictory" although they could both be true, or that some information appeared only after I spent a minute agonizing over which similar data chunk is least incorrect), this is a very finely crafted portrait of surveillance and its moral implications. Even as someone pro-privacy and personal freedom, I found myself thinking "This is justifiable since it's for the good and safety of innocents".
Then the ending cutscene I got was about 30s long, yet somehow I'm still recovering.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Long story short: I would recommend this game. That being said, I had a lot of criticisms--so forgive me if the rest of this seems self-contradictory. There are plenty of other reviews that thoroughly cover what the game does well. 

After the intriguing trailer, I found the first two episodes dissappointing. The art style was clean and pleasant as expected, but I found the characters to be boring and slightly unlikable, which prevented much investment in the story. 

However, the game does shift as you progress through later episodes--interesting developments, twists, overturned expectations. It wasn't phenomenal, but I did get invested, and found the whole experience ultimately worth purchasing.

My biggest problem with the game--some of it felt like a trudge through data files, rather than the investigative puzzle I hoped for. The few times I was prompted with a high stakes question, where my answer actually mattered, I felt like I had to find the answer through mindless clicking, rather than any logic or puzzle solving. It felt a little pointless, honestly.

In sum, I felt like the game didn't quite live up to its potential--although there were definitely moments where I felt for the characters, and was confronted with the discomfort and ethical ambiguity of violating their privacy. I was put in tense situations, was surprised, and had some control over the course of events. Despite my disappointment in the beginning, I really enjoyed the final episodes. So that's why I would recommend this game--Orwell has a novel premise that was executed fairly well, and it's defintiely an experience worth having.
